values.articles-body:
Every morning I write a list, and every evening about half of it is still there. For years I read that as a small daily failure. I now think the half-finished list is the most honest document I produce, and that learning to read it is worth more than learning to finish it.

## What the list is actually for

A to-do list pretends to be a plan. It is really a record of what caught my attention between waking and sitting down: the email I remembered in the shower, the errand that surfaced while making coffee, the one piece of real work I meant to do yesterday. Written down, those items look equal. They are not. Some of them are the day's work and some are noise that happened to arrive early.

The list does its best job before I start. Writing an item down lets me stop holding it in my head, and that release is the whole point. A list that is never finished has still done that job perfectly. The trouble begins when I treat it as a contract rather than a place to set things down.

## Reading what is left

At the end of the day I no longer count the crossed-out lines. I look at what survived and ask one question of each item: *why is this still here?*

The answers fall into a few groups.

- **It was never mine to do today.** It depended on someone else, or on a decision that had not been made. It belongs on a different list, or nowhere.
- **It was smaller than it looked, and I avoided it anyway.** These are the interesting ones. A five-minute reply that sits for a week usually hides a conversation I do not want to have.
- **It was larger than it looked.** "Draft the proposal" is not a task; it is a project wearing a task's clothes. It stays because it cannot be crossed off in one sitting, and it will stay tomorrow too unless I break it apart.
- **It was the real work, and I did something easier.** This is the one to be honest about.

Sorting the leftovers this way takes three or four minutes. It tells me more about how I spent my attention than any tracking tool I have tried.

## The cost of carrying items forward

The easy move is to copy everything unfinished onto tomorrow's list. I did this for a long time, and the lists grew until the first ten items were a museum of things I had once meant to do. Each one asked for a flicker of attention every time I read past it. None of them got done, because none of them were chosen; they were simply inherited.

Now nothing moves forward automatically. Each surviving item has to be rewritten by hand, which is slow on purpose. If an item is not worth ten seconds of pencil, it is not worth a place at the top of tomorrow. Some days I rewrite two things and let the rest go. Nothing bad has happened yet.

## Finishing less, choosing more

The half-finished list changed how I plan. I now write the one item that matters first, and I draw a line under it. Everything below the line is welcome to be forgotten. On a good day the thing above the line is done by noon and the rest is a bonus. On a bad day the line is still a clear statement of what I was supposed to protect.

This sounds like a productivity trick. It is closer to a habit of attention: a daily moment where I look at what I said I cared about and compare it with what I actually did. The gap between those two is not a failure to be closed. It is information, and the list is where it shows up in my own handwriting.

If you want a place to start, try this tonight. Do not finish your list. Read it. Ask each leftover why it is still there, and write only the honest answers onto tomorrow's page. The rest of this journal is, in one way or another, about [what to do with the attention that frees up](/articles/a-desk-with-one-thing-on-it).

articles-cover.articles-cover-alt: A handwritten to-do list with half its items crossed out and a pencil across it
articles-cover.articles-cover-caption: A morning list at six in the evening.

values.articles-intro: Half of every to-do list survives the day. Reading what is left, instead of counting what is done, turns out to be the useful part.

values.articles-author-bio: Teodor trained as a joiner and now works mostly in text. He writes about tools, maintenance and the craft of doing one thing well.
values.articles-body:
The first thing I was taught at a woodworking bench was not how to cut. It was how to sharpen. My teacher put a dull chisel in my hand, a whetstone in front of me, and a jar of water beside it, and said we would start the real work when the edge could shave the hair on my forearm. That took most of an afternoon.

I resented it at the time. I had come to make a box. Years later it is the lesson I use most, and hardly ever at a bench.

## A dull edge hides its cost

A dull chisel still cuts. That is the problem. It crushes the wood fibres instead of slicing them, so every stroke needs more force, and more force means less control. The cut wanders. You push harder to correct it, and the edge slips. Nothing about the tool announces that it is the cause; it simply feels as if the work is difficult and you are not very good at it.

Most of the tools I use now are not steel. They are a text editor, a notebook, a calendar, a way of naming files, a small set of habits for starting a day. Each of them can go dull in exactly the same quiet way. A shortcut I never learned. A folder structure that made sense three projects ago. A template full of sections nobody fills in. The work still gets done, with a little more force than it should need, and I blame the work.

## Sharpening is a separate act

The discipline my teacher was really teaching was the separation. You do not sharpen in the middle of a cut. You stop, put the workpiece down, and give the edge your full attention for ten minutes. Then you go back to cutting and give that your full attention too.

I try to keep the same boundary with non-steel tools. When I notice that something is fighting me, I write it on a card instead of fixing it on the spot. Fixing it immediately feels efficient but breaks two kinds of focus at once: the task I was doing, and the repair, which deserves better than a distracted five minutes. On Friday afternoons I take the cards out and sharpen. I rename the folders. I delete the template sections. I learn the one shortcut I have reached for twenty times this week.

## How to tell when an edge is ready

At the bench, the test is simple and physical: the edge catches on a fingernail, or it does not. With other tools I use a rougher test. After sharpening, the next use should feel almost boring. If I still have to think about the tool while doing the task, it is not sharp yet; if I only think about the task, it is.

A few questions help me find the dull edges:

1. What do I do every day that takes more than three steps?
2. What do I avoid starting because the setup is annoying?
3. Where do I keep correcting the same small mistake?

The answers are rarely dramatic. They are almost always cheap to fix, which is exactly why they go unfixed for so long.

## Not an excuse to stop working

There is a trap here, and woodworkers know it well: the person who sharpens forever and never cuts. A perfect edge is satisfying in a way that finished work often is not, because it asks nothing of your judgement. I have lost weeks to rebuilding a note-taking system instead of taking notes.

My teacher's rule protects against that as well. You sharpen until the edge passes the test, and not a stroke more. Then you cut. The point of a sharp tool is that it disappears in your hand and leaves your attention for the wood.

> Sharpen before you cut, and stop sharpening when it cuts.

That is still the most useful sentence anyone has said to me about work. It pairs well with Teodor's later note on [choosing tools you can repair](/articles/choosing-tools-you-can-repair), because an edge you can maintain yourself is one you will actually keep sharp.

articles-cover.articles-cover-alt: A wet whetstone beside a chisel on a wooden bench
articles-cover.articles-cover-caption: Ten minutes at the stone, then back to the wood.

values.articles-intro: The first lesson at a woodworking bench was an afternoon at the whetstone. It is still the lesson I use most, and rarely on steel.

values.articles-body:
For about a month I kept only one thing on my desk at a time. Not one kind of thing, one object: a notebook, or a laptop, or a book, or a single printed page. Everything else lived on a shelf across the room. It started as an experiment after a bad week and became the way I work.

## What a crowded desk asks of you

I used to think of my desk as neutral. Objects sat on it; I ignored the ones I was not using. It turns out I was not ignoring them at all. Each one was a small unfinished sentence. The unopened letter said *deal with me*. The stack of books said *you were going to read these*. The second notebook said *you started something else, remember?*

None of these requests was loud. Together they made a steady background hum that I only noticed when it stopped. The first morning with a bare desk felt strangely quiet, the way a room does when a fridge you had stopped hearing switches off.

## The rules I settled on

The rules were simple, and I broke them often enough to learn why they mattered.

- **One object on the desk.** A pen counts as part of a notebook; a cup of tea does not count at all.
- **To change objects, walk.** Putting the notebook back on the shelf and fetching the laptop takes perhaps twenty seconds. That short walk turned out to be the point.
- **Nothing is stored on the desk overnight.** The desk starts each morning empty, and the first decision of the day is what to put on it.

The walk was the part I resisted and the part that changed the most. Switching tasks at a crowded desk costs nothing, so I did it constantly, sometimes every few minutes. When switching meant standing up and crossing the room, I noticed each switch. Often I noticed it before I stood up, and sat back down.

## What changed

The obvious result was fewer interruptions of my own making. I had assumed most of my distractions came from outside: messages, noise, other people. A good share of them came from the objects in my peripheral vision, each quietly offering an easier task than the one in front of me.

The less obvious result was that choosing became visible. With one object on the desk, the question *what am I doing right now?* always has a physical answer. If the answer is the laptop, I know I chose the laptop. If I find myself reading the news on it, I can see the gap between the choice and the behaviour, and that gap is easier to close when it is not hidden among six other things.

It also made the ends of tasks cleaner. Putting the notebook back on the shelf is a small ceremony that says *this is done for now*. I had never had that before. Work used to trail off rather than stop.

## What it is not

A bare desk is not a moral position, and I do not think clutter is a character flaw. Some work genuinely needs several things at once: a reference open beside a draft, a sketch next to a model. When that happens I clear enough space for the task and nothing more, and I put it all away when I stop.

It is also not about the desk. The desk was just the easiest place to see a pattern I had everywhere: on my screen, in my calendar, in the [list I carry through the day](/articles/the-half-finished-list). One thing in front of me, chosen on purpose, everything else a short walk away. I keep coming back to that shape.

If you try it, give it a week. The first two days are uncomfortable. By the fifth, a crowded desk starts to look like a room full of people all talking at once.

articles-cover.articles-cover-alt: A bare wooden desk with one closed notebook in the centre

values.articles-intro: For a month I kept a single object on my desk. The short walk to swap it for another changed how often I switched tasks.
values.articles-title: A desk with one thing on it

values.articles-body:
I take a lot of notes. For a long time almost none of them were ever read again. They went into apps, into notebooks, into files called *misc*, and they stayed there like letters posted to an address nobody checks. A few years ago I started asking a narrower question than "how should I take notes?" The question was: which of my notes are still useful a week later, and what do they have in common?

## Most notes are for the moment

The honest answer is that most notes should not survive the week, and that is fine. A phone number scribbled during a call, a list of points for a meeting, a sketch of an idea I am about to try: these do their work within hours. Keeping them forever does not make them more valuable; it just buries the few that matter under a growing pile.

So the first change was to let most notes die. I use a single pad of scrap paper for anything temporary, and the pad goes into the recycling every Friday without being reviewed. That one habit removed a surprising amount of guilt. The notes that belonged to the moment were allowed to stay there.

## What the survivors look like

The notes I still reach for after a week share a few traits.

**They make sense to a stranger.** The stranger is me, eight days later, without the context I had when I wrote them. "Fix the header thing" is useless by Thursday. "The header wraps below 400px because the logo has a fixed width" is still useful a year on.

**They hold one idea.** A note that contains a meeting summary, two unrelated ideas and a shopping list is hard to find and harder to use. A note that holds one idea can be moved, grouped, and combined with others.

**They say why.** A note that records a decision without its reason ages badly. The decision gets questioned, nobody remembers the reason, and the argument happens again. One extra sentence—*because the supplier only ships on Tuesdays*—saves the whole conversation.

**They are written, not captured.** Pasting a paragraph from somewhere else is capture. Restating it in my own words is writing. Only the second one tells me, later, that I understood it.

## Index cards

These traits pushed me toward a very old tool: the index card. A card is small enough that it can only hold one idea, and it is physical enough that writing on it feels deliberate. At the end of each week I go through the scrap pad and the week's meeting notes and ask whether anything deserves a card. Usually two or three things do. I write them out properly, in full sentences, with the reason included, and file them in a box by topic.

The box is not clever. There are no links, tags, or search. There are about a dozen dividers, and cards move between them when I reorganise my thinking. Pulling one card out of a stack and reading it in isolation is the fastest way I know to find out whether a note was written well.

## The weekly pass is the whole system

I have tried many note systems, and I now think the tool matters much less than the pass. Any system works if you regularly sit down, read what you wrote, and decide what to keep. No system works if you never do.

My pass takes about twenty minutes on a Friday, often in the [quiet hour](/articles/the-quiet-hour) before anyone else is around. Scrap pad in the recycling, meeting notes skimmed, two or three new cards written, one old card reread at random. That last step is my favourite. Sometimes the card is obsolete and goes in the bin. Sometimes it is exactly what I needed that week, and I have no idea how I forgot it.

The notes that survive the week are the ones I chose to keep, written for someone who was not there. That someone is always me.

articles-cover.articles-cover-alt: A stack of index cards in a binder clip with one card pulled out
articles-cover.articles-cover-caption: The week's keepers, one idea per card.

values.articles-intro: Most notes should be thrown away by Friday. The few that deserve to last have a few things in common, and a box of index cards holds them well.

values.articles-body:
When I share an early draft, I make it look early on purpose. Pencil instead of ink. Plain text instead of a laid-out document. Grey boxes where the pictures will go. It is not modesty and it is not laziness. How finished something looks changes the conversation people are willing to have about it, and in the early stages I want the rougher conversation.

## Polish invites the wrong kind of feedback

Show someone a beautifully typeset page and they will comment on the typesetting. They will notice that a heading is slightly too large, that two paragraphs have uneven spacing, that a word is misspelled in line four. All of that is real, and almost none of it matters yet. The questions I actually need answered—*is this the right argument? does the structure hold? is anything missing?*—get crowded out, because the page looks as if those questions were already settled.

A pencil sketch sends a different signal. It says the big decisions are still open. People feel free to say "what if the whole middle section went first?" because moving it costs nothing. The same suggestion made about a polished draft feels rude, and often goes unsaid.

## Finish is a promise

Every layer of finish implies a decision. Choosing a typeface implies the words are settled enough to be worth setting. Adding real photographs implies the layout is fixed. Tidy margins imply the content fits them. When I polish too early, I make those promises before I have earned them, and then I defend them longer than I should, because I have already invested the time.

There is a quieter cost too. Polishing is pleasant. It feels like progress and asks very little of the hard part of the mind. I have spent whole mornings adjusting the look of a draft whose second half did not yet make sense, and called it work. An unfinished-looking draft removes that temptation. There is nothing to polish, so the only thing left to do is think.

## Keeping the marks visible

The most useful drafts I keep are the messy ones: pages with lines struck through, arrows moving paragraphs, questions in the margin. I used to tidy those marks away before showing the draft to anyone. Now I leave them. The crossings-out show where I changed my mind, which is often where the interesting decisions were made. The margin questions tell a reader exactly where I am unsure, so they can spend their attention there instead of on the parts I am confident about.

A few habits help me keep drafts honest about their state:

1. **Match the finish to the question.** If I am asking about structure, I share an outline. If I am asking about tone, I share a few paragraphs. I only share a laid-out page when I am asking about the layout.
2. **Say what kind of feedback I want.** One line at the top—*looking for problems with the argument, not the wording*—saves everyone time.
3. **Leave placeholders obvious.** A grey box labelled *photo of the workshop* is better than a stock image that someone will mistake for a choice.

## When to switch

None of this means drafts should stay rough forever. There is a point where the big questions really are settled, and then finish becomes the work. Spacing, word choice and image selection deserve full attention once the argument is sound, and they deserve it from someone who is not still arguing with the structure.

The skill is noticing the moment of the switch. My test is simple: when I stop moving paragraphs around, the draft has earned some polish. Until then, it should look exactly as unfinished as it is. The same idea runs underneath Mina's piece on [the half-finished list](/articles/the-half-finished-list): showing the true state of the work is kinder, to other people and to yourself, than pretending it is further along.

values.articles-intro: How finished a draft looks decides what people will say about it. Early on, pencil and grey boxes invite the conversation that matters.

values.articles-body:
I get up an hour before I need to. Not to exercise, not to answer email early, not to squeeze more work into the day. The hour has no task attached to it at all. I make tea, sit in the chair by the kitchen window, and let my attention settle before anyone else gets a claim on it.

It is the most productive hour of my day, and I do almost nothing in it.

## Attention has a morning state

For most of the day my attention is spoken for. Messages arrive, meetings start, other people's priorities fill the gaps between my own. By mid-morning I am responding more than choosing. That is not a complaint; responding is a large part of any job. But it means the hours when I could think freely are few, and they are almost always at the edges of the day.

Early morning is the widest of those edges. Nothing has happened yet. There is no thread to follow, no reply I am waiting for. The mind, left alone, starts to wander toward whatever it has been quietly working on. Often that turns out to be the problem I could not solve yesterday.

## What I do with the hour

Very little, by design. The rules are these:

- **No screens.** The phone stays in another room until the hour ends. This is the only rule that is not negotiable.
- **No agenda.** I do not plan to think about anything in particular. If a problem shows up, I let it. If nothing does, I look out of the window.
- **Something to write with.** A notebook and pencil sit on the sill. I rarely write more than a few lines, but when a thought arrives I want to catch it before the day washes it away.
- **The same place.** The chair, the window, the cup. Doing it in the same spot every day makes it easy to slip into without deciding to.

Some mornings I read a few pages of a book. Some mornings I just watch the light change on the wall opposite. Both count.

## Why it pays off

The hour works because it gives my attention a chance to find its own level before the day pulls it somewhere else. Ideas that need slow thinking—how to structure a long piece, what to say in a difficult conversation, whether a project is worth continuing—rarely come to me while I am busy. They come when there is room for them.

It also changes the rest of the day. Starting from quiet, I am more likely to choose the first real task deliberately instead of reaching for whatever is loudest. The [one thing I put on my desk](/articles/a-desk-with-one-thing-on-it) at eight o'clock is usually something I decided on in the chair at seven.

## Protecting it

The hour is easy to lose. One early meeting, one late night, one morning of checking the phone "just for a second," and the habit starts to slip. I protect it the way I would protect an appointment with someone else. If the hour has to move, it moves; it does not disappear.

I also try not to make it into another task. The moment the quiet hour becomes a place to *get things done*—clear the inbox, plan the week, study—it stops working. Its value is precisely that nothing is expected of it.

You do not need a full hour, and you do not need the morning. Twenty minutes at the end of the day works for some people. The only requirements are that nobody else can claim the time, and that you do not claim it for anything either. Sit somewhere comfortable, put the screen away, and see where your attention goes when you stop telling it where to go.

articles-cover.articles-cover-alt: An empty chair beside a window at dawn with a steaming cup on the sill
articles-cover.articles-cover-caption: Seven o'clock, before anyone else has a claim on the day.

values.articles-intro: An hour before the day begins, with no task attached to it. It is the most productive hour I have, and I do almost nothing in it.

values.articles-body:
My fountain pen is older than I am. It belonged to my grandfather, and it has been taken apart, cleaned, and put back together more times than anyone has counted. Last winter the feed cracked, and I ordered a replacement for a few coins, fitted it with a small screwdriver on the kitchen table, and was writing again the same evening. Almost every other tool I own would have gone in the bin.

That repair made me look at the rest of my tools with a new question. Not *is this good?* but *when it breaks, can I fix it?*

## Repair is a kind of understanding

A tool you can take apart is a tool you can understand. You can see how the ink travels from the reservoir to the nib, which part wears first, and what a small adjustment does. That understanding changes how you use it. You notice early signs of trouble. You stop blaming yourself for problems that are really mechanical, and you stop blaming the tool for problems that are really yours.

A sealed tool offers none of that. When it misbehaves, the only options are to accept the behaviour or replace the whole thing. Over time you stop paying attention to how it works at all, because there is nothing you can do with the knowledge. The tool becomes a black box you depend on without understanding.

## The same question for digital tools

This matters just as much for software, where most of my working hours are spent. A few questions help me judge whether a digital tool is repairable in the sense I care about:

1. **Can I get my work out in a plain format?** Text files, standard images, a folder I can open without the tool. If the only way to read my notes is through one application, that application owns them.
2. **Can I change the parts that bother me?** Settings, templates, shortcuts, small scripts. A tool that lets me adjust it to my habits is one I will keep sharp.
3. **Will it still work if the company behind it disappears?** Tools that depend entirely on a remote service can vanish overnight. Tools that run on my own machine, with files I hold, tend to last.
4. **Is it simple enough to learn completely?** I would rather use a small tool I understand fully than a large one I understand in patches.

None of these rule out modern or convenient tools. They just make the trade visible. Sometimes the sealed option is worth it. But I want to choose that, not drift into it.

## Fewer, better, maintained

Choosing repairable tools has left me with fewer of them. That was not the goal, but it follows naturally. Repairable tools need care, and I only have attention to care for so many. So I keep a small set: the pen, a plain text editor, a paper notebook, a box of [index cards](/articles/notes-that-survive-the-week), a chisel set that I [sharpen on Fridays](/articles/sharpen-before-you-cut). Each one gets regular maintenance, and each one feels better in the hand for it.

The maintenance itself has become part of the work I enjoy. Cleaning a pen takes ten minutes and leaves my mind clearer than it found it. Tidying a set of text templates does something similar. These small acts of care keep me connected to the tools, and through them to the work.

## A modest test

Next time a tool breaks, before replacing it, spend ten minutes finding out whether it can be fixed. Look for a part number, a manual, a forum where someone else has had the same problem. Sometimes the answer is no, and that is useful to know when you choose the next one. Sometimes the answer is a spare part that costs less than a coffee and an evening at the kitchen table.

Either way, you will understand the tool a little better than you did. That understanding is the real thing a repairable tool gives you, and it lasts longer than the tool itself.

articles-cover.articles-cover-alt: A fountain pen disassembled into parts on a cloth beside a small screwdriver
articles-cover.articles-cover-caption: Every part of a pen that outlived its first owner.

values.articles-intro: A cracked pen feed, a few coins and an evening at the kitchen table. A tool you can fix is a tool you understand.

Last year I read fewer books than in any year since university, and I remember more of them than I have in a decade. The change was not a new app or a reading challenge. I simply started reading slowly, on purpose, with a pencil in my hand and no target for how many pages to get through.

## Speed was hiding the problem

For years I read quickly because I thought quantity was the point. There were always more books on the list than time to read them, so I skimmed, skipped, and finished. At the end of the year I could list the titles. If you had asked me what any of them argued, I would have struggled.

Fast reading felt efficient because it produced a visible result: another book done. What it did not produce was understanding. The ideas passed through without catching on anything. I was treating reading like clearing an inbox, and getting about as much out of it.

## What slow reading looks like

Reading slowly does not mean reading every word at half speed. It means giving the book the kind of attention I would give a person I was talking to. In practice, a few habits:

- **One book at a time.** Juggling five meant none of them got my full attention. Now one sits on the table and the rest wait on the shelf.
- **A pencil, always.** I mark sentences that surprise me, write questions in the margin, and argue with the author when I disagree. The marks are for me, not for posterity.
- **Stop at the end of a chapter and say what it was about.** Out loud, or in two lines in the back of the book. If I cannot, I read the last few pages again.
- **Reread the good parts.** When a passage is dense or beautiful, I read it twice before moving on. This felt wasteful at first. It is now the part I look forward to.
- **Let myself stop.** A book that is not worth slow reading is not worth fast reading either. I put it down without guilt.

## The ribbon bookmark

My favourite small tool for this is the ribbon bookmark sewn into some hardback books. A loose bookmark falls out and gets lost; the ribbon stays. It sounds trivial, but it changed how I finish a reading session. Before closing the book, I lay the ribbon across the page at the exact line where I stopped. The next time I open it, I begin by rereading the paragraph before the ribbon, which drops me straight back into the author's line of thought.

That small ritual of ending and resuming turns a book into a long conversation rather than a series of disconnected sittings. It is the same instinct behind the [quiet hour](/articles/the-quiet-hour): give the attention a clear place to start, and it settles faster.

## Reading as craft

Slow reading turned out to be a skill, and like any craft it improves with practice. At first I was impatient, constantly checking how many pages were left. After a few months the impatience faded. I began noticing how writers built their arguments, where they were careful and where they were bluffing, which sentences did the real work. Those observations have fed back into my own writing more than any style guide.

It also changed what I choose to read. When each book costs more attention, I am pickier about which ones earn it. The list has become shorter and better. I reread old favourites more often, and find something new in them nearly every time.

## Try one chapter

You do not need to overhaul your reading life. Pick the book you are currently reading, take a pencil, and read the next chapter as slowly as it asks to be read. Mark what surprises you. When you reach the end, say in two lines what it was about. Then close the book and notice how much of it stays with you.

For me, that was enough to stop counting.

values.comments-body: Asking "why is this still here?" instead of counting what got done is such a small change. I tried it last night and found three items that were never mine to do.
Rewriting leftovers by hand is the part I'll steal. Copy-paste made my list a museum too.
"Stop sharpening when it cuts" is going on a card above my desk. I lose far too many afternoons rebuilding my setup instead of using it.
The Friday card box for dull edges is a lovely idea. Fixing things mid-task always costs me twice.
As a furniture maker I can confirm the forearm test. The rest of the essay made me look at my inbox rules differently.
The walk across the room is the genius part. Friction in the right place instead of none anywhere.
Letting the scrap pad go to the recycling without review sounds terrifying and freeing at the same time. Trying it this Friday.
We started sharing wireframes in pencil after reading this, and the feedback moved from button colours to whether the page should exist at all. Exactly right.
Mine is twenty minutes on the balcony after the kids are asleep. Same rules, same effect.
No agenda is the hard part. I keep trying to turn it into planning time and it stops working immediately, just as you say.
"Can I get my work out in a plain format?" should be the first question for every piece of software. Thanks for the checklist.
Saying what a chapter was about before moving on has doubled how much I keep. Five books this year so far, and I can talk about every one.

values.about-body:
![A bare wooden desk with one closed notebook in the centre](/uploaded-assets/asset-assets-8eb1c7be-6575-4ab5-9570-387c3c496145 "Where most of these essays start.")

Margin Notes is written by Mina Okafor and Teodor Lindqvist. Mina writes mostly about attention: the lists, desks and reading habits that decide where a day goes. Teodor writes mostly about tools and craft: sharpening, repairing, and the notes that make work repeatable.

## What we write about

Every essay is short enough to read in one sitting and tries to leave you with one thing to try. The three threads run into each other constantly:

- **Craft** — how good work gets made, slowly and on purpose.
- **Attention** — where it goes, and the small habits that protect it.
- **Tools** — choosing, maintaining and repairing the things we work with.

## How often

Roughly one essay a fortnight. If you would rather have them arrive than come looking, [the Sunday note](/newsletter) sends the newest one each week.
